name: range-v3
baseline: hand-written loop building a std::vector<std::string> (the 'handrolled' row of the issue's benchmark); the issue's 'algorithm' row is a further baseline whose code is not shown
workload: Google Benchmark of a lazy views::transform | views::common pipeline (append '!' to palindromic words) over a list of about 476k words, copied into a std::vector<std::string>, against a hand-rolled version and an 'algorithm' version.
claimed_speedup: Time per iteration, from the table in issue #1337 (reporter's machine): at -O2 range_common 10,816,578 ns vs handrolled 12,443,168 ns (about 13% less time, derived from page data) and vs algorithm 25,840,577 ns (about 2.4x faster, derived from page data); at -O3 range_common 9,305,111 ns vs handrolled 9,594,576 ns (about 3% less time, derived from page data) and vs algorithm 21,961,494 ns (about 2.4x faster, derived from page data). The ranges::to variant in the same table is slower than hand-rolled: 23,025,614 ns at -O2 and 21,293,927 ns at -O3 (the issue's subject).
compiler_and_flags: Compiler not stated in the issue; -O2 and -O3 (binary names benchmark-palindromes-o2 / -o3); Google Benchmark
hardware: No CPU model named; Google Benchmark header 'Run on (2 X 2684.42 MHz CPU s)' for the reporter, '8 X 2900 MHz CPU s' for the maintainer's run
tradeoffs: Header-only C++14/17/20 library. Views are lazy and non-owning, so lifetime of the underlying range is the caller's problem. Offers more adaptors than std::ranges (actions such as sort/unique/shuffle, extra views). Heavy template machinery: Niebler attributed slow cases to view_adaptor being hard for optimizers (issue #668). Conversion with ranges::to (a range-v3 extension) was about 1.8x (-O2) to 2.2x (-O3) slower than hand-rolled in the same issue's benchmark, derived from page data (issue open since 2019).
caveats: Weak evidence for a speed win. The numbers come from a bug report titled 'ranges::to is significantly slower than direct construction', not from a project claim; the README makes no performance claim and publishes no numbers (its perf/ directory holds benchmark sources only, no results). The win over hand-rolled code is one workload, 13% at -O2 and 3% at -O3 (likely noise level) on a 2-core machine; the compiler is not stated and the bodies of the handrolled and algorithm functions are not shown in the issue, so what they do is unknown. The issue dates from 2019-09-29, so the library version predates current releases. The maintainer's own run (8 CPUs at 2900 MHz, -O3) only compared Words/RangeCommon 201,502,562 ns with Words/RangeTo 241,609,633 ns, no hand-rolled row. No comparison against std::ranges was found. Reachable third-party results go the other way: the transrangers README (Clang 11.0, GCC 11.1, VS2019, GitHub Action VM, flags and CPU not stated) says range-v3 is consistently outperformed by handwritten code on Clang and performs very badly on its concat|take|filter|transform test; issue #668 says partial_sum_view was about half the speed of the STL approach (no compiler or flags). Lead from the books: no timings are given there. Treat as tier C with low confidence.
found_via: seed-record pass: started from https://github.com/ericniebler/range-v3 (README, perf/ directory, doc/), then WebSearch 'range-v3 benchmark faster than std::ranges OR hand-written loop views::filter transform results nanoseconds github' surfaced issue #1337; also opened issue #668 and the transrangers README

name: zoo (thecppzoo) zoo::VTableFunction / zoo::Function
baseline: std::function (with a shared_ptr wrapper for the move-only capture, since std::function cannot hold a move-only callable)
workload: Third-party Google Benchmark harness in tenstorrent/tt-metal PR #57569: construct, invoke and destroy a move-only capture at 16-byte inline capacity, plus queue throughput over 1024 jobs and compile time and object size, for std::function, zoo::VTableFunction<2, void()> and fu2.
claimed_speedup: BM_MoveOnlyCapture median ns, std (shared_ptr) vs zoo: gcc-12/libstdc++ 42.69 (3 allocs) vs 13.43; clang-20/libstdc++ 43.29 vs 14.00; clang-20/libc++ 45.64 vs 12.72 (about 3.2x, 3.1x and 3.6x faster, derived from page data); commit message: 'both candidates are about 3x faster on a move-only capture and cut 3 allocations to 1'. Queue throughput, 1024 jobs, std vs zoo (unit as printed in the README table): 5519 vs 5074, 6633 vs 5610, 7068 vs 5697 (about 1.09x, 1.18x and 1.24x, derived from page data). Compile time, best of 3, std vs zoo: 3.67s vs 3.58s, 2.79s vs 2.53s, 7.46s vs 2.88s. Object text size std vs zoo: 5229 vs 3111, 3256 vs 2114, 3633 vs 2108. Construct/invoke/destroy of a plain small capture: 2.3-3.2 ns for all three, so no win there.
compiler_and_flags: gcc-12 with libstdc++, clang-20 with libstdc++, clang-20 with libc++; C++20; harness CMakeLists defaults CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to Release when unset and sets no other explicit optimization flags; google-benchmark v1.9.1, fu2 4.2.5, zoo pinned at commit 7fb5eed6331651e9d94c0f7e9017f2d56ba4b993 (harness commit b28acab)
stars_or_usage: 139 stars; the author's presentation says its type-erasure framework ran in production at Snapchat
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 (MSVC supported but occasionally buggy per the README). Policy-based inline buffer and ownership (zoo::AnyContainer, AnyCallable, Function), so capacity is a template choice; zoo::function is AnyCallable<Any, Signature>. Per the tt-metal evaluation: sizeof grows from 24 to 32 bytes under libstdc++ (40 vs 48 under libc++); does not build under -fno-rtti; its move vtable entry is noexcept but accepts throwing-move targets, which would terminate; needed a roughly 45-line wrapper to satisfy tt-metal's compliance checks. The README's CppCon 2022 note says the implementation it released may not be production-ready.
caveats: Evidence is independent but not the project's own: the repo's benchmark/catch2Functions.cpp compares zoo::function against std::function, folly::Function and a function pointer but publishes no numbers, and the README and design docs contain none (design/AnyContainer.md says 'pending concrete benchmarks'). The 3x figure is against std::function plus a shared_ptr workaround for a move-only capture, an idiom gap (C++23 std::move_only_function is the fair baseline), and the benchmark measured zoo::VTableFunction<2, void()>, not zoo::Function itself. CPU model not stated in the pages read; flags are only the Release default. The harness commit messages carry a Claude co-author line, and the PR says results were later moved to a PR comment after a harness rerun, so the commit-time numbers may be superseded. tt-metal did not adopt zoo: PR #57569 ships an in-house move_only_function that adapts zoo's buffer-plus-table layout, and the PR table (42.94 ns vs 12.96 ns on gcc-12) measures that in-house type, not zoo, so it is not used here. Queue-throughput gains are small (9-24%). The book lead matches the repo only by author name. Category changed from small-buffer-and-strings to smart-pointers-and-refcount because the compared facility is std::function (spec Part 3 map).
